t.6.11.1: Having spoken these harsh words to Rāvaṇa, Rāvaṇa's younger brother came within a moment to the place where Rāma was with Lakṣmaṇa.
t.6.11.2: Standing on the earth, those lords of the monkeys beheld him poised in the sky, shaped like the peak of Meru and gleaming like blazing lightning.
t.6.11.3: Seeing him with four companions, himself the fifth, Sugrīva, the wise and unassailable lord of the vānaras, deliberated together with the vānaras.
t.6.11.4: Having reflected for a moment, he spoke these excellent words to all those monkeys led by Hanūmān.
t.6.11.5: Look! This rākṣasa, equipped with every kind of weapon, is approaching together with four other rākṣasas to kill us, there is no doubt.
t.6.11.6: Having heard Sugrīva's words, all those foremost of the vānaras raised up sāla trees and rocks and spoke these words.
t.6.11.7: Quickly command us, O king, to slay these wicked-souled ones; struck down, let these whose lives are short fall upon the earth.
t.6.11.8: While they were conversing with one another, Vibhīṣaṇa reached the northern shore and stood there, remaining in the sky.
t.6.11.9: And the great and supremely wise Vibhīṣaṇa, still standing in the sky, looked closely at Sugrīva and the others and spoke in a loud voice.
t.6.11.10: There is a rākṣasa named Rāvaṇa, wicked in conduct, the lord of the rākṣasas. I am his younger brother, known by the name Vibhīṣaṇa.
t.6.11.11: By him Sītā was carried off from Janasthāna after he had slain Jaṭāyuṣa; and having confined her, helpless and wretched, he has her closely guarded by rākṣasīs.
t.6.11.12: With reasons and with words of many kinds I pointed out to him again and again: "It is right that Sītā be returned to Rāma."
t.6.11.14: Spoken to harshly by him and treated with contempt like a slave, I have abandoned my sons and my wife and have come to Rāghava for refuge.
t.6.11.13: But Rāvaṇa, driven on by Time, would not accept the beneficial words spoken to him, just as a man whose condition has turned against him refuses medicine.
t.6.11.15: Quickly announce me, Vibhīṣaṇa, who have arrived here, to the great-souled Rāghava, the refuge of all the worlds.
t.6.11.17: The younger brother of Rāvaṇa, known by the name Vibhīṣaṇa, has come to you for refuge together with four rākṣasas.
t.6.11.16: Having heard these words, Sugrīva, swift in his valor, spoke thus to the agitated Rāma in the presence of Lakṣmaṇa.
t.6.11.18: Know that this Vibhīṣaṇa has been sent by Rāvaṇa. I consider it fitting that he be seized and restrained, O best among the forbearing.
t.6.11.19: This rākṣasa has come here, dispatched with crooked intent and concealed by illusion, to strike you down once you have come to trust him, O Rāghava.
t.6.11.20: Let this one be bound, together with his ministers, under severe punishment, for this Vibhīṣaṇa is the brother of the cruel Rāvaṇa.
t.6.11.21: Having thus spoken to Rāma, who was skilled in speech, the agitated commander of the army, himself versed in discourse, then fell silent.
t.6.11.22: Having heard those words of Sugrīva, the mighty Rāma spoke thus to the monkeys standing near him, headed by Hanumān.
t.6.11.23: The exceedingly well-reasoned speech that the king of the monkeys spoke concerning Rāvaṇa's younger brother has been heard by you all as well.
t.6.11.24: For in difficult affairs it is fitting for a friend who is wise and capable, and who desires lasting prosperity, to offer counsel.
t.6.11.25: Thus questioned, they, alert and eager to do what was beneficial, then courteously told Rāma each his own opinion.
t.6.11.26: There is nothing in the three worlds unknown to you, O Rāghava. Honoring yourself, O Rāma, you ask us out of friendship.
t.6.11.27: For you are true to your vows, heroic, righteous and firm in valor; you act only after careful consideration, you are mindful, and you have given yourself wholly to your friends.
t.6.11.28: Therefore let your ministers, endowed with wisdom and capable, speak one by one, giving their reasons again and again.
t.6.11.29: When this had been said to Rāghava, the wise monkey Aṅgada, standing in front, then spoke these words for the purpose of testing Vibhīṣaṇa.
t.6.11.30: Having come from the presence of the enemy, he is surely to be suspected in every way; Vibhīṣaṇa must not hastily be made one worthy of trust.
t.6.11.31: For those of deceitful mind go about concealing their true nature, and they strike at weak points; that would be a very great calamity.
t.6.11.32: Having first determined what is beneficial and what is harmful, one should then resolve upon a course of action. One should accept a person on account of his merits, but cast him off on account of his faults.
t.6.11.33: If there is a great fault in him, let him be cast off without hesitation; or else, if you find many virtues in him, let him be taken in, O king.
t.6.11.34: Then Śarabha, having considered the matter, spoke words full of meaning: "O tiger among men, let a spy be quickly set upon him."
t.6.11.35: Only after properly setting a spy of keen intelligence upon him and examining him should acceptance then be granted, in accordance with what is right.
t.6.11.36: Then Jāmbavān, the discerning one, having carefully considered the matter with an understanding grounded in the śāstras, submitted counsel that was full of merit and free from fault.
t.6.11.37: Vibhīṣaṇa has come from the lord of the Rākṣasas, who is wicked and with whom enmity is bound, at the wrong place and time; let him be suspected in every way.
t.6.11.38: Then Mainda, skilled in sound policy and its opposite and gifted in speech, having reflected carefully, spoke words even more firmly grounded in reason.
t.6.11.39: O lord of the best of men, let this Vibhīṣaṇa be questioned gently and slowly about the very words of that Rāvaṇa.
t.6.11.41: Then Hanūmān, the foremost of counsellors, endowed with refinement of speech, spoke words that were gentle, meaningful, sweet and concise.
t.6.11.40: But having first understood his true disposition, you will then do what is fitting, O bull among men, once it has been carefully ascertained whether he is wicked or not.
t.6.11.42: Not even Bṛhaspati, were he to speak, would be able to surpass you, who are foremost in wisdom, capable, and the best among speakers.
t.6.11.43: Not out of mere argument, nor from rivalry, nor from any sense of superiority, nor from desire, O king, but out of my high regard for Rāma, I shall speak words that are true.
t.6.11.44: In what your counselors have said concerning the grounds of advantage and disadvantage, I see a flaw, for such a course of action is not feasible.
t.6.11.45: Without assigning him a task, his ability cannot be known; yet assigning him one suddenly seems to me a mistake.
t.6.11.46: As for what your ministers have said, that it is proper to employ spies, there is no ground for it, since the purpose cannot be achieved that way.
t.6.11.47: As to the point that this Vibhīṣaṇa has arrived at the wrong place and the wrong time, I have something to say on this matter; hear it, according to my understanding.
t.6.11.48: Just as this very place and time come to be thus or otherwise here, passing from one man to another, so too do faults and virtues.
t.6.11.49: Having seen the wickedness in Rāvaṇa and likewise the valor in you, his coming here is fitting and worthy of his intelligence.
t.6.11.50: O king, as to what has been said, that he should be questioned by men whose identity is unknown, on this matter I have a certain well-considered view.
t.6.11.51: Questioned abruptly, a wise man would grow suspicious of the words. In that case one would alienate a friend who had come in good faith, by questioning him falsely.
t.6.11.53: But no trace of evil intent is ever seen in him as he speaks, and his face too is serene; therefore I have no doubt.
t.6.11.52: Truly, O king, it is impossible to know suddenly the feeling that lies within another, even for one who keenly observes, with great skill, the true nature revealed in those words he has spoken.
t.6.11.54: With an untroubled mind and at ease, he does not approach like a deceiver, nor is his speech at all corrupt; therefore there is no doubt in this matter.
t.6.11.55: One's outward appearance, even when it is being concealed, cannot be fully hidden, for it forcibly reveals the feeling that lies within men.
t.6.11.56: O best among those who know what must be done, one quickly brings to fruition a task that is suited to the place and time and undertaken with the proper means.
t.6.11.58: Seeking the kingdom, he has come here deliberately; keeping just this in view, it is fitting that he be received.
t.6.11.57: Having observed your undertaking and seen Rāvaṇa acting falsely, and having heard of the slaying of Vālin and of Sugrīva consecrated as king…
t.6.11.59: I have spoken as best I can about the rākṣasa's sincerity; but you, O best of the wise, having heard this, are the authority on the rest.
